person.name: André Korobeinikoff
person.laterName: André Korbey (also recorded as Andre Korby)
person.summary: Born to a peasant family in the Voronezh region of Russia; imprisoned as a young man during the unrest of 1905; studied engineering in Belgium; served with a British-organised medical relief unit in Serbia in 1915; settled permanently in England, married, raised three children, and became a naturalised British subject in 1935.

sources.title: Family memoir (handwritten account, author unnamed — written by a descendant's wife)
sources.notes: Written well after the events described, likely decades later, based on family recollection rather than contemporaneous records. Warmest and most detailed on the early Russian/Siberian/Balkan period, which no official record corroborates.

sources.title: Metropolitan Police Special Branch report on naturalisation application, 15 October 1935
sources.notes: Based on a formal interview with André himself plus corroborating referees, bank records, and police files. The most contemporaneous and fact-checked source, but focused on residence/character/finances relevant to naturalisation — it is silent on Siberia and on any 1905 exile beyond a term of imprisonment.

sources.title: Serbian 'Cross of Mercy' (Krst milosrđa) certificate, issued in the name of King Peter I of Serbia
sources.notes: Awarded for care of wounded and sick soldiers in the wars of 1912 and 1913 — note this predates WWI service and may relate to the Balkan Wars, or be a general-service Red Cross-type award issued during his 1915 Serbian service.

sources.title: Imperial War Museums, 'Lives of the First World War'
sources.type: curated public record aggregating multiple archival sources
sources.notes: Aggregates a Medal Index Card, British Red Cross volunteer transcription, marriage index, 1939 Register, Mabel Stobart's own published account, and the National Archives naturalisation certificate reference. Licensed under the IWM Non-Commercial Licence — review before public reproduction.

waypoints.title: Born at Repetz, Voronezh province

location.name: Repetz (Repetz village), Voronezh province, Russia
location.locationConfidence: approximate — pinned to Voronezh city as the nearest identifiable point; exact village not located

waypoints.description: Born on a peasant farm. A good singing voice won him a place at a Monastery school and later a Grammar School education.

waypoints.title: Military call-up and imprisonment during the 1905 unrest

location.name: Russia (exact location not recorded)
location.locationConfidence: unknown — no location given in any source

waypoints.description: Called up for military training during the period of the Russian revolution of 1905. Sentenced to a term of imprisonment for taking part with other soldiers in preparing and presenting a petition to his commanding officer, contrary to regulations.
waypoints.note: The family memoir frames this same period as being 'sent to Siberia as a political prisoner' following involvement in student political activity leading up to what it calls 'the Karensky revolution' (almost certainly 1905, not Kerensky/1917). The 1935 police report — based on André's own sworn statement — describes a military petition and imprisonment but does not mention Siberia at all. Both cannot be fully reconciled from what survives.

waypoints.title: Siberian exile and Arctic escape (family account only)
waypoints.dateConfidence: estimated — 'I believe this journey took several years' (memoir), bounded by the 1905 imprisonment and his documented 1911 departure to Belgium

location.name: Siberia — exact location unknown
location.locationConfidence: family-oral-history-only — this pin is a best-guess placeholder near the Ob Gulf, one of the standard western Siberian exile regions in this period, not a documented location

waypoints.description: Family account: sent to Siberia as a political prisoner with a number of fellow students. He and a few others spent a long time preparing to escape — studying the tides of an Arctic sea inlet, getting fit, storing provisions — and in Spring attempted a crossing using their knowledge of the tides and their ability to swim and float. André was one of the few who succeeded.
waypoints.note: No official record confirms Siberian exile. Two real historical patterns fit the story: (1) western Siberian political exile near the Ob River/Arctic coast, the same region Trotsky was being sent to around this time before his own escape near Berezov; or (2) the Kola Peninsula/Murman coast in Russia's European Arctic, a well-documented escape route to Norway via Vardø, which better matches a narrow, tidal, swimmable inlet. Family memory may simply be using 'Siberia' loosely for 'the far north.' Treat this waypoint as illustrative, not factual, on the map.

waypoints.title: Reached Albania

location.name: Albania — exact point of arrival unknown
location.locationConfidence: approximate — centred on Albania generally; no specific town given

waypoints.description: Family account: after the escape, André eventually reached Albania, then worked his way north toward Belgium.
waypoints.note: Intriguingly, André was later awarded an 'Albanian Commemorative Medal' in 1920 (see the 'albanian-medal' waypoint below) for otherwise-unspecified war service. It's plausible the family's 'reached Albania' story has become entangled over time with this documented medal, or that there is a genuine independent Albanian connection the medal is only partial evidence of. Worth investigating further before treating either as settled.

waypoints.title: Left Russia; studied engineering at Liège
waypoints.description: In 1911 he left Russia for Belgium. He was a student at Liège University until the outbreak of war. The family account adds that he also acquired a working knowledge of medicine somewhere along the way.

waypoints.title: Worked as a hospital dresser near Liège

location.name: Near Liège, Belgium
location.locationConfidence: approximate — 'a hospital near Liege', exact institution not named

waypoints.description: Following the outbreak of war he worked as a dresser at a hospital near Liège until 1 December 1914.

waypoints.title: Arrived in the United Kingdom as a refugee

location.name: Earls Court refugee camp, London, UK

waypoints.description: Arrived in the UK on 20 December 1914 with other refugees from Rotterdam and remained at a refugee camp at Earls Court until April 1915.
waypoints.note: The family memoir instead frames this as obtaining 'a permit to travel to Russia via England' in 1915 while still in Belgium — a softer framing than the official record's account of fleeing as a war refugee. Likely the same episode, remembered differently.

waypoints.title: Served with Mrs Stobart's medical unit in Serbia
waypoints.dateConfidence: documented — corroborated independently by the police report, Mabel Stobart's own published account, and his Red Cross record card

location.name: Serbia (region '2a')
location.locationConfidence: approximate — pinned to Belgrade; the specific towns Mrs Stobart's unit operated in during the 1915 retreat are not given in the sources to hand

waypoints.description: Went to Serbia as a dresser and hospital orderly with Mrs Stobart's Unit — 3rd, under the Serbian Relief Fund's 'Other Empire Force.' Held a diploma from the Joint Committee of the British Red Cross Society and the Order of St John of Jerusalem for valuable service during the war.
waypoints.note: The family memoir dates this service to 'most of 1916' — but three independent, more contemporaneous sources agree on April–December 1915. This is very likely a minor error in family memory rather than a real discrepancy.

waypoints.title: Registered address while serving with the relief fund

location.name: c/o Miss Diblee, 25 Margareta Terrace, Chelsea, London

waypoints.description: Recorded 'away from home' address in 1915, likely an administrative or correspondence address connected to the Serbian Relief Fund rather than a residence.

waypoints.title: Awarded the Serbian Cross of Mercy
waypoints.description: Awarded the Krst milosrđa (Cross of Mercy) in the name of King Peter I of Serbia, for care given to wounded and sick soldiers in the wars of 1912 and 1913.

waypoints.title: Senior clerk, Russian Relief Committee
waypoints.description: Employed as senior clerk in the permit section of the commercial department of the Russian Relief Committee. Obtained exemption from Russian military service in 1917 — fortunate timing, given the Russian Revolution that year.

waypoints.title: Studied electrical engineering at Birmingham University
waypoints.description: Took a course in electrical engineering.

waypoints.title: Wound up the affairs of the Russian Relief Committee
waypoints.description: Employed in a clerical capacity winding up the Russian Relief Committee.

waypoints.title: Married Enid Pyemont
waypoints.description: Married Enid Pyemont, a British-born subject. Her family — the Oldrinis of Beeston, Nottinghamshire — is a separate genealogical thread worth following up.

waypoints.title: Awarded the Albanian Commemorative Medal

location.name: Not specified
location.locationConfidence: unknown — award record gives no location

waypoints.description: Awarded the Albanian Commemorative Medal, classed as an 'Other War Service Award.'
waypoints.note: See the note on the 'albania' waypoint above — possible (unconfirmed) connection to the family's Albania escape story.

waypoints.title: Ran a jewellery-making business

location.name: London, UK (home address)
location.locationConfidence: approximate — home address at the time not specified

waypoints.description: Earned his living making articles in metal, silver, and decorative stones into Russian peasant designs, worked from home.

waypoints.title: Accountant, All Union Textile Syndicate / Arcos

location.name: King William Street, then Wilson Street, then Bush House, Strand, London
location.locationConfidence: approximate — pinned to Bush House, his last known office there

waypoints.description: Worked as secretary and later accountant for the All Union Textile Syndicate, absorbed into Arcos in 1927. Discharged in July 1932 amid reorganisation, after declining a verbal suggestion that he return to Russia.

waypoints.title: Established tobacco/cigarette-machine business
waypoints.description: Became a wholesale tobacconist, installing and servicing cigarette machines in private houses; ran the business from his home address. By 1935 he had roughly 300 customers.

waypoints.title: Naturalised as a British subject
waypoints.description: Naturalisation certificate granted (HO 334/139/6649), following a favourable Special Branch report dated 15 October 1935. Later changed the family name from Korobeinikoff to Korbey.

waypoints.title: Died at Anerley
waypoints.description: Died at Anerley, Kent — the same address, 4 Selby Road, where he had lived and run his business since 1932.

waypoints.title: A descendant sees his picture in Belgrade

location.name: Kalemegdan Fortress, Belgrade, Serbia
location.locationConfidence: documented — named directly in the memoir

waypoints.description: The memoir's author recounts a family visit to Yugoslavia, where her husband's work took him, and seeing a photograph of Mrs Stobart's medical mission — including André — displayed at a museum believed to be at Kalemegdan, one of the oldest fortifications in the country.
waypoints.note: This is not part of André's own life timeline — it's a later family episode. Consider handling it on the site as an epilogue/postscript rather than a stop on his personal journey map.
